She had picked the hour before dawn for her attack on purpose. Naturally. Had last night passed without incident, and had I gone to bed as usual, she could have walked up to my pillow and I would not have noticed.

The leader closed the distance by one slow step. The arrogant ease of last time was gone without a trace.

What remained was composure, backed by real ability.
—Yes. She was strong.

That impression renewed, I abandoned the plan of fighting with the back of the blade. Fighting that way, I could never win.

A sword is made to put its edge on the enemy. This is not only a matter of sharpness. Shape, weight balance, the winding of the hilt cord, the placement of the menuki—everything assumes that use.

Ignore it and you cripple the sword's performance. With the gap in strength already there, taking on a further handicap would send my slim chance away before I even got my hand on it.

So: handle the tachi correctly, and miss the vital points. Failing that, stop the stroke just short.

...Either way, I judged it hardly easier than winning with the back of the blade. But if a choice moved me even one sheet of thin paper closer to victory, I was responsible for making it.

This back of mine carried a fate bigger than my own life.

Inch by inch, the leader slid the soles of her feet across the ground and closed the distance. A tortoise's pace—and that very slowness was the threat.

To walk this slowly, slower and slower, without disturbing posture or center of gravity is a truly extraordinary feat. Holding posture is far easier at speed.

Consider a bicycle. Riding fast is one thing. Now ride slower than a walking man, without losing balance. Who finds that easier?

Her slow feet meant that feat: complete control of her center of gravity. A fear older than thought crawled up my spine, cold.

...In other words, with this footwork she could command, exactly and without waste, the instant when the distance entered cutting range, and deliver one stroke at the best possible moment.

To stand against that, I had to catch the same moment myself. I barely managed to calm my eyes as tension stiffened them, loosened them just enough, and steadied my field of vision.

My feet stayed where they were.
That too was a choice.

I could answer her footwork with footwork of my own, disturb her hold on the distance and take it for myself. That road existed. I abandoned it. Challenge her there and I would most likely lose.

In a fight over distance, battle experience speaks louder than anything. A few years of military service and a handful of formal matches—I had not the slightest belief that they could match a Rokuhara warrior's seasoned campaigns.

Stand still, and I concede the initiative. Very well. In return, I get the easier measurement of distance. She is moving, however slowly; I am not. On that point, the advantage belongs to me.

I would find my chance there, or nowhere.

　姿勢を、重心を、崩さぬままに遅く遅くゆっくりと
ひた歩むのはまさに至難の業だ。
　姿勢の維持は早足の方が遥かに易く済む。

　自転車を例に引き出せば自明の事。
　歩くよりも遅い速度で自転車を乗りこなすなど、誰
にできようか？

　首領の遅足は、その離れ業を――重心の完全制御を
意味している。
　本能的な怯えが、俺の背筋を冷たく這い登った。

　……つまりはこういう事だ。
　彼女はこの歩法により、間合が<ruby>斬り間<rt>・・・</rt></ruby>に達する瞬間
を、ずれなく無駄なく完全に掌握し、最高の機に一刀
を繰り出す事ができる。

　これと拮抗するには、同じ戦機をこちらも掴むしか
ない。
　俺は緊張に強張りかける眼球を辛うじて宥め、適度
に弛緩させて視野を安定させた。

　足は、その場に留める。
　これも一つの選択であった。

　敵の歩法に対してこちらも歩法にて応じ、敵の間合
掌握を乱し己のみ間合を奪おうと図る――それも一途。
　だが放棄した。そこに勝負を挑んではおそらく勝て
ない。

　間合の取り合いとなれば、何よりも実戦経験が物を
言う。
　高々数年ばかりの兵役と幾度かの仕合の経験のみで、
六波羅武者の歴戦ぶりに敵し得るとは些かも思えない。

　静止して待てば、間の取り合いについてはアドバン
テージを譲ることになるものの、距離の把握において
はこちらの方が容易であり優位となる。微速ながらも
敵は動いている以上、この点は揺るがない。

　そこに勝機を見出すに如かず。

No breath showed in the morning mist, so her breathing was completely invisible to me. And mine? Was I hiding it as cleverly... or not?

Letting your breath be read is about the same as writing your schedule of actions on a blackboard and holding it up for the enemy. She would catch the instant I could not respond to, and come.

The body is moved by muscle, and muscle output depends on the state of the breath. As a rule, breathing out produces more power than holding, and holding more than breathing in.

So she must never, under any circumstances, detect the moment I draw air into my lungs—the instant every muscle in my body loses some of its capacity to act. The remedy is to ease the force of my exhale as far as I could.

Hide the exhale and the inhale hides too.
The lungs are best used quietly...

Before I knew it, the distance had narrowed.

The distance between us, shaved down as if with the tip of a small knife, was approaching a certain value.

—A certain value.

That is, the distance at which one must cut.

I let the chance go. Perfectly still, I let her keep closing the distance.

The stretch where I could cut and she was still beyond her own out of range—my zone of advantage was not long. It would be lost soon. That I was watching it go by seemed to offend her.

...Understandably.
By the ordinary rules of strategy, I should have struck by now.

What held me back was one word snagged in my mind.

Correctly speaking, it was the Rokuhara branch of Yagyuu Shinkage Style. It descended from the great school that was once the Tokugawa house's own. Its founder was a certain Yagyuu who, at the end of the Tokugawa era, dropped his master, threw himself in with the Court faction, and came under Rokuhara's command.

It has so many peculiar techniques of its own that calling it Yagyuu Style at all is doubtful, yet it flourished inside the Shogunate army. A branch, and still it outranks the main house; its head even takes a seat in the Shogunate cabinet from time to time.

The current head is Jouansai Yagyuu. They call him a master the like of whom comes once in an age, and for that skill he is said to lead the Rokuhara Umayashuu, the Ashikaga clan's personal escort—no. None of that matters here.

Standing beside Yagyuu Shinkage as the school entrusted with the Tokugawa house's military arts is Ono-ha Itto Style. Also a famous school, and its secret teaching is especially renowned.

Kiriotoshi.

...I could not claim that the leader—that Shinkage Style—did not know this principle. Ono and Yagyuu served the same lord and treated each other as potential enemies; stealing techniques from each other was reportedly everyday business.

Even without that, it is nothing rare for one school's technique to exist under another name in a different school. They all pursue the handling of the same weapon, so no wonder. Nothing would be odd about Rokuhara Yagyuu transmitting Kiriotoshi.

In fact, that is exactly why I know the principle and not only the name. In the Yoshino style, this technique is transmitted under the name Uchi-shio.

If the leader answered my attack with Kiriotoshi instead of racing me in sword speed, the contest would become a mutual reading of sword lines. When two dropping cuts clash, the sword that gets read ends up dropped.

And that contest favors her. Since I would be the one attacking, I would already have fixed more than half my sword line by then. Changing mid-stroke is not impossible, but the room for it is narrow and small.

Against an opponent who moves after seeing part of my sword, there is an edge that cannot easily be overturned. It is said that one who masters this sword may draw but never lose—hence the awe it inspires as the supreme art of a sword saint.

en.html:
That is why I let the chance pass. The danger that the leader knew Kiriotoshi, or something like it, an intercepting technique that grants the first strike and wins afterward, I could not bring myself to dismiss as unworthy of consideration.

............Perhaps I had let my only winning chance slip away. I shook off the doubt crawling restlessly around my heart and measured the distance afresh.

My zone of advantage was ending. One breath more, and we would be in mutual striking range.

Right now I had three options. One: attack from my superior distance. Two: attack at mutual striking distance. Three: wait at mutual distance for the enemy to attack.

The opponent, naturally, had options to match.

First option. Attack from my superior distance—if she answered with a technique like Kiriotoshi, I lost. If not, the difference in sword speed won it.

Second option. Attack at mutual distance—if she attacked as well, no one had the advantage; sword speed decided. If she waited for a counter, I lost.

Third option. Wait for her attack—if she came as I wished, I won, provided my skill could carry the Striking Tide principle through. If she did not come, nothing moved.

Each road had its merit and its flaw. The deciding point was what I feared most in the enemy.

If I feared her sword speed most, I must attack now, while I could start first. Once in mutual range, the best I could get was equal or worse.

If instead I set her counter-technique as the greatest threat, the first and second options were gone. I must choose the third: the waiting posture.

Which danger was I choosing to fear?
...A question for which I had already supplied the answer.

だから見送った。
　首領が切落ないしはそれと同質の術、相手に先制を
許しながら後より勝つ迎撃技法を心得ている危険性に
ついて、考慮に値せずとは思い切りかねた。

　…………もしかすると、俺は唯一の勝機を逃したの
かもしれない。
　心臓の周辺に<ruby>ざわざわ<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>と蠢く迷いを振り捨て、気を
新たに間合を測り直す。

　俺の優越距離は終わりかけていた。
　あと一呼吸後……双方の<ruby>打ち間<rt>レンジ</rt></ruby>となる。

　現在この時点で、俺には三つの選択肢があった。
　優越距離で仕掛けるのが一。相互攻撃の距離で仕掛
けるのが一。相互攻撃の距離で敵が仕掛けて来るのを
待つのが一。

　これに対応する形で、相手の側にも選択肢があると
いうことになる。

　まず第一の選択。
　こちらの優越距離で仕掛けた場合――相手が切落の
ような技をもって応じるなら、こちらの敗となる。
　そうでなければ剣速の差で勝。

　第二の選択。
　相撃の距離で仕掛け――相手も同様に仕掛けて来た
なら優劣は無し。剣速で勝敗は決する。
　敵が切落を期して待ち構えたなら敗。

　第三の選択。
　敵の仕掛けを待ち――望み通りに敵が来たならば勝。
〝打潮〟の剣理を俺の技量で全うできるなら、だが。
　敵が来なかったなら、状勢は動かず。

　いずれの方途も一長一短。
　選択の決め手は、敵の何を最も恐れるかという判断
だった。

　運剣の速度を最も恐れるとするなら、先にスタート
を切れる今こそ仕掛けねばならない。
　相互攻撃の間合に入った後では、互角以下の勝負に
しかならないのだ。

　そうではなく、迎撃技を最大の脅威と設定するなら、
第一・第二の選択は無いということになる。
　選ぶべきは第三。待ちの姿勢だ。

　どちらか。
　……だが、この決断は既に下している。

Even in this shape, there was room to choose. Besides waiting artlessly for the enemy to change her mind, there were other roads.

One: both withdraw. When a contest falls into this form, the mannerly warrior acknowledges the other's skill and calls it a draw.

Another: offer bait. Appear to attack, draw out her counter so it hits empty air, then subdue her afterward.

Either could break this deadlock. And I could choose neither.

The second also did not deserve consideration. If I had judged her someone who would swallow an obvious feint, I had plenty of simpler ways to act before getting stuck this far.

But I dismissed my own idea. The instant I retreated, my body would be helpless.

I would lose the driving force to advance and strike. For her, that would be the chance. No counter to fear, and with my weight flowing backward, my defense would have no footing either. Cutting me down would be easy.

To believe she would fail to seize that chance was naive. She could not have forgotten to count retreat among the moves open to her opponent—to me.

If I fell back, she would certainly bite.

...No escape.
Not even a plan for buying time.

Time simply piled loss on loss and drew me closer to the hour of my death.

The distance at which the tachi in my two hands would become meaningless was approaching.

...After all, I never meant to kill this opponent. Losing killing power could be accepted, in itself.

But to hope that the loss of striking force would settle neatly below killing force and above subduing force—that was a selfish hope.

Having killing power means being able to cut through bone.
Not having it means being unable to cut bone.

If the distance kept being invaded and we came to blows—even if my greater speed got my edge to her body first—my tachi would bite some centimeters into her shoulder.

But she would not stop. A hundredth of an instant later, her blade would arrive, cut me through bone and organs, and kill me.

Defeat.

Then: not a trade of strokes, but a one-sided blow? Even if one blow could not decide the match, could it weaken her and turn the flow my way?

If I sealed her sword by the principle of Striking Tide, the Dropping Cut, and then struck? Or, by using body movement, evaded her one stroke...

All my effort was just zero piled on zero, and nothing useful came of it. The malicious swell trying to wash my mind and body away did not weaken even as a consolation; it sneered, and got its way.

The feeling went first from below.
...My hips and legs were gone.

They had vanished somewhere.
No, impossible—if I looked down they would surely be there.

But I could hardly let my eyeballs do as they pleased. The enemy was in front of me...!

With desperate effort, I fixed my gaze forward every time it threatened to drop. Yet by doing so, I could not dispel the idiotic suspicion that my hips and legs did not exist.

Now even whether I was standing was doubtful.
I felt as though I were floating in the air.

Holding a tachi, dancing through the sky...
Then I am exactly like a warrior, I thought, in something like a dream.

A warrior would not be much troubled even if both legs truly vanished. They are merely components for posture control, so to speak.

I had to step in with my feet,

My cutting interval was not lost. It was maintained.

The leader must have felt it. Her not cutting at once was the best proof.

All I had done was shift my center of gravity.

My feet stayed where they were. I changed the angle of both knees and moved my hips slightly back—weight to the rear, but only by a hair, not enough to let my body flow away.

That finished the change.
From a posture for stepping in to cut to a posture for cutting on the spot.

It was the form of the practice swing I knew so well. A warrior's training for fighting in the sky, which deliberately seals the footwork.

On the ground, normally, a swing form with no practical meaning. In a fight with footing, it only means foolishly throwing away the benefit of a step.

Normally.
In a situation like this one, with the enemy deep inside my guard, the folly reverses.

It produces the effect of shortening the cutting distance. That was the road to seize one life out of ten thousand deaths.

At this distance, with her deep entry received, I who had given up the step was still in perfect position: the spacing at which my striking section would catch her.

Once thought of, it was extremely simple. But the fixed belief that a cut means stepping in had not let that simple idea in easily.

I felt as though I were holding my whole body at the edge of a cliff with one finger.

—Not that I had time to sigh in relief.

I had left the killing ground.
And the situation now reached its limit.

The leader saw my transformation and showed no hesitation about her course. She kept up the slow advance, perfected to an extreme.

In the present state, I was at a distance where I could do nothing but cut. Yet I still could not attack carelessly.

Her limbs were shorter than mine, so she kept some margin in her distance. Even this close, she could use Kiriotoshi or some other answering technique. ...I still had to wait.

Whereas she stood in a position like mine at the start. I had no room to counter. The only answer was a mutual strike. So her best play was to move at once, and get her sword to me even one hair sooner.

But—she did not come.
She only shaved the distance and measured my breathing.

Why?
I could not say for sure.

But perhaps this, too, came from pride in herself. Rather than a paper-thin victory, did she want a complete one, by threatening me into attacking and countering it?

The killing intent thickening each moment certainly fanned my fear. If I loosened the reins of my mind even a little, I might start screaming and swing wildly at once.

Holding back the impulse took every bit of my will.

—A little more. I had to endure only a little more.

The last milestone would come soon.

The distance would keep narrowing,
until my opponent too reached the range where she could only cut.

No room left for either of us to prepare an answering technique.
Only cut and cut, a contest of sword speed.

No strategy, no art, no technique.
Conditions even. Beyond doubt, an equal match.

Which is faster?
Which is stronger?

One exchange of swords would decide it.

The last milestone.
The last chance.

...Distance: close.
My enemy stood within reach of an outstretched hand.

Her face was—◆
still as the surface of a lake.

She was a bandit. A former Rokuhara soldier with a history not worthy of respect, a woman I disliked by any measure.

But at this very moment she was a pure warrior—and nothing else.

A single-minded force to defeat the enemy called me.

　確たるところは、定かではない。

　しかし、あるいは……これも己への自負心ゆえか。
　紙一重の勝利よりも、俺を威迫し誘い出しての迎撃
による完勝をこそ望むのか。

　確かに刻一刻と厚みを増す殺気は俺の恐怖心を煽り
立てる。
　精神の手綱をほんの少しでも緩めればその瞬間にも、
喚き立てながら無闇に斬り掛かってしまいそうな程に。

　衝動を堪えるには意志力の総動員を必要とした。
　
　――あとわずか。あとわずか、耐えねばならない。

　最後の節目が間もなく訪れる。

　間合はこのまま狭まり……
　遂に敵手も、ただ斬るばかりの距離に達する。

　互いに応じ技を凝こらす余地、最早なく。
　ただただ斬り合い、剣速を競うのみの間合に。

　策も術も技も無し。
　条件は五分と五分。疑いようもなく互角の勝負。

　どちらが、速いか。
　どちらが、強いか。

　一刀の振り合いにて、それを決する。

　最後の節目。
　最後の戦機だ。

　……間合は近接。
　手を伸ばせば届くほどの距離に、我が敵はいた。

　その貌は、◆
　――湖面の如く。

　彼女は山賊だ。
　六波羅上がりの、尊敬できぬ経歴を持つ、どう見た
ところでいけ好かない女だ。

　しかし今この瞬間は、純一の武人であって――ただ
それきりの存在だった。

　湊斗景明おれという敵に打ち克つ、
　ひたむきなちから。
